items.title: Move live memory to Postgres and keep vector search in ClickHouse
items.body:
### Component

Memory and search

### Use case

Loom needs to support frequent point reads and writes alongside tenant-scoped retrieval and scans over billions of records. These workloads should not all use the same write path.

A memory write needs ordered versions, compare-and-set, locks and pin checks. ClickHouse serves retrieval and analytics, but its part creation and merge costs make individual committed inserts a poor fit for this workload. [#129](https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/pull/129) batches several request-path tables; it leaves the main memory tables committed.

The sizing assumptions are 5,000 tenants, 50,000 namespaces, 1,000–50,000 memory writes/sec and up to 10,000 user searches/sec. These are design inputs, not measured capacity or production traffic. If all 50,000 writes need a semantic conflict check, that adds 50,000 retrievals/sec before user search, extra retrieval legs or background work. At a sustained 50,000 writes/sec, the system also produces 4.32 billion write events/day.

Quality is the highest priority: retrieval and admission verdicts must use the right revisions, preserve tenant and access boundaries, and retain the evidence needed for recovery. Scalability and low end-to-end latency are required alongside that quality. Optimize cost and component count only within those guarantees; do not trade away recall, durability or access checks to meet a throughput number.

The goals are point reads without a second database lookup, transactional writes, fresh search results, and bounded ingest and retention costs. Postgres and ClickHouse are the only databases. All stored vectors and vector search stay in ClickHouse. The sizing inputs describe a deployment spread across placement units; they are not a promise that one Postgres primary or one namespace sustains the aggregate peak.

### Describe the solution you'd like

#### Storage ownership

Postgres stores current memory content, not just its latest version and hash.

| Workload | Storage |
| --- | --- |
| Current memory content, metadata, versions, locks, pins and compare-and-set | Postgres |
| Working memory, task state, idempotency and delivery claims | Postgres |
| Identity, grants, revocation and mutable namespace configuration | Postgres |
| Revision journal and enrichment jobs | Postgres, retained until their required deliveries complete |
| Embeddings, lexical and vector retrieval, searchable metadata and derived graph projections | ClickHouse |
| Historical revisions, conversation archives, audit queries, usage and rollups | ClickHouse |
| Large immutable code-index artifacts and compiler graph generations | ClickHouse |

Every live record has one authority. Preserve `(org, namespace, agent, user_id, session_id)`, stable record identity, source revision, actor, source class and attestation through both stores. The server derives provenance from the authenticated writer and operation. Org-wide identifiers must still pass the same scope checks without revealing another tenant's records. A ClickHouse projection cannot grant access to a record Postgres refuses.

The Postgres transaction atomically records current content, the complete immutable revision, required delivery jobs, the idempotency state and a hash-only mutation audit event. Keep mutable delivery progress separate from revision payloads so job updates do not replicate the content again. A search document is a derived serving representation, not the revision journal or the audit record. Required audit events are durable before the audited operation completes; best-effort usage metrics have a separate delivery contract.

Keep the existing ClickHouse-only install path for smaller deployments. This proposal defines the Postgres+ClickHouse path. Record the selected authority and reject replicas configured for a different one; an outage must not silently switch a deployment between them.

#### WalShadow replication and enrichment have different jobs

Use [ClickHouse Managed Postgres](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres) with [WalShadow](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres/sync-to-clickhouse/walshadow) for selected database mirrors and revision events. WalShadow is the first implementation path. Loom should not build a general WAL transport or run two writers into the same destination projection.

Build and test the replication path with WalShadow. Judge it by source load, replication lag, payload correctness and recovery under Loom workloads. Its private-preview status alone is not a reason to defer implementation or choose ClickPipes. A documented or reproduced limitation that blocks a required guarantee is a release blocker, not an accepted reduction in quality. Replication benchmarks are not a latency guarantee for a Loom operation.

Pin the evaluated WalShadow build and replication configuration. Its documented limits include failure to continue after an unplanned primary promotion and unresolved large-value reconstruction cases. Validate complete revision payloads, including large text and JSON values, against source hashes through initial load, updates, cleanup and restart. A selected value mode that can substitute missing or incorrect bytes does not qualify for archival delivery. Keep WalShadow as the first implementation path, resolve blocking limitations, and reconsider the transport if it cannot satisfy the required guarantees ([limits](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/544c340d17039d2b24068897c6f616b9e67e1ac6/docs/limitations.md), [failover protocol](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/544c340d17039d2b24068897c6f616b9e67e1ac6/docs/failover.md)).

Replicate an explicit allowlist of tables and columns. Destination identities must distinguish source placement units, databases and tenants, including during a tenant move. Mutable configuration mirrors serve analytics, not authorization. Account for WalShadow recovery state and large-value mirrors in capacity, access control, backup and erasure inventories.

Loom still needs enrichment jobs. CDC does not generate embeddings or decide when a revision is searchable. These jobs read committed revisions directly from Postgres and publish search documents into ClickHouse without first waiting for the CDC mirror.

A search document carries its source revision, content hash, embedding-model and preprocessing versions, chunk identity, text and filter metadata. Reuse an embedding only when its input and model contract match. A worker can rebuild the document from a retained revision or its confirmed archive. Vectors never pass through Postgres tables or its revision journal.

Readiness is recorded only after every projection required by that operation is delivered and visible. Optional graph or analytics work does not delay a write unless its contract requires it. Lexical publication can precede embedding completion, but it must not mark semantic search ready or weaken ordinary `memory.set` success semantics.

#### Writes and point reads

For a semantic `memory.set`:

1. Validate the value and access scope. Start embedding work and the required search-freshness check concurrently.
2. Check duplicates, conflicts and protected memories against sufficiently fresh state.
3. In a short Postgres transaction, recheck the key version and relevant guards, update current content, and record the complete revision and required jobs.
4. Publish the required search projection directly into ClickHouse.
5. Return success after the operation's promised visibility is satisfied.

Do not hold a database transaction open during inference or ClickHouse queries. Reuse embeddings computed during admission, and reuse existing embeddings for metadata-only changes.

Postgres handles same-key compare-and-set atomically. For cross-key semantic admission, capture a generation for every scope whose state can change the verdict and wait for its required search projections. Every relevant creation, update, pin, blacklist, access-policy or model-manifest change advances the corresponding generation in the mutation transaction. After inference and retrieval, compare those generations again in the short commit transaction and advance them with the write. Checking only returned candidate versions misses a peer created while the check was running. A Postgres isolation level alone does not track predicates evaluated in ClickHouse. Recheck time-based expiry and lock leases at commit; a generation does not track the passage of time.

Enforce pinned and blacklist protections separately from approximate result ranking. A contract that refuses peers above a similarity threshold needs a complete check over eligible protected peers; an ANN or quantized shortlist alone cannot prove that no protected peer matches. Evaluate the false-accept and false-refusal rates of semantic verdicts as well as retrieval recall.

Use a deterministic lock order across affected scopes, bounded retries and one request deadline. Batch admissions within busy conflict scopes, including interactions between writes in the batch; vector comparisons still execute in ClickHouse. A namespace-wide invariant still needs namespace-wide coordination; do not split that scope or omit checks to claim horizontal scalability. Measure its sustainable rate and reject excess work explicitly before queues grow without bound.

`memory.set` and `bulk_set` keep their inline verdicts, including pinned refusals. Deferred ingestion is a separate contract that reports pending enrichment. Ordinary transactional operations that need no semantic work finish at the Postgres commit.

A crash after that commit leaves a durable revision and a repairable job. Scope idempotency to the authenticated caller and operation, bind it to a request digest, and replay it only after current authorization. Reusing a key with different input is rejected. A projection timeout returns the committed revision, operation identity and pending state; a retry resumes that revision instead of admitting a second mutation. Specify status lookup, cancellation after commit, idempotency retention, expired-key behavior and the HTTP, MCP and SDK responses before changing the write path.

`memory.get` reads current content directly from Postgres. Strict current reads, final authorization and admission guards use the primary; replicas serve other reads only when their replay position meets the request's consistency requirement.

#### Retrieval and visibility

Strict search captures a finite committed barrier for its authorized scopes when admitted, including any caller-supplied write dependencies, then checks that the selected ClickHouse reader can serve the required projections. Later writes do not keep moving that barrier. This promises coverage through the captured barrier, not an atomic snapshot across the two databases. Current access and deletion checks still apply, and concurrent content changes can require bounded refill or an explicit incomplete result. Any weaker consistency mode is an explicit API contract, never an automatic timeout fallback.

Several writes share one visibility wait at a dependent search. Track a completed prefix with gaps or an equivalent durable manifest; event allocation order and the largest observed revision do not prove that earlier work committed or finished. A superseded revision can be resolved only when the protocol proves that its required serving effect is covered. An insertion acknowledgement or a readiness row on one replica is not proof for every reader. Bind the proof to the actual tables, serving generation and reader; re-establish it after rerouting or replica changes ([ClickHouse read consistency](https://clickhouse.com/docs/resources/support-center/knowledge-base/data-management/read-consistency)).

Track committed state and searchable readiness separately. Readiness includes the source revision, model version and reader visibility. A replication cursor or `max(event_id)` is not enough. WalShadow documents that different tables from one Postgres transaction can become visible in ClickHouse at different times ([consistency limits](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/main/docs/limitations.md#ordering-and-consistency)).

Retrieve lexical, semantic, entity and temporal candidates in ClickHouse. Apply tenant and known eligibility filters inside every retrieval leg, then batch-check candidate revisions, permissions, expiry and deletion state in Postgres before exposing snippets or sending content to an external reranker or answer model. Never attach current content to a score computed from an older revision. Apply the same checks to graph expansion, context assembly, caches, traces, exports and history APIs; an analytical mirror is not an access authority.

Candidate validation cannot recover a relevant revision absent from the search projection. Discard obsolete candidates, deduplicate by source identity and revision, and refill within bounded rounds, rows, bytes and time. Report readiness failures, refill exhaustion and missing required retrieval legs as explicit unavailable or incomplete outcomes. Do not label a truncated pool a complete empty result or let an answer model present it as complete evidence. Define authorization and revision check points for external dispatch and final response, and revalidate when the relevant access generation changes during a long request.

Tenant policy controls external model use and content egress. Partition result and model caches by access scope, source revisions, model and serving generation. Revocation and erasure invalidate affected entries; raw ClickHouse tables and `pg_clickhouse` must not expose an alternative route around these checks.

Keep the existing retrieval path as the baseline. Small eligible sets use tenant-scoped exact scans or an evaluated quantized shortlist with original-vector rescoring. Large tenants get dedicated placement and serving capacity.

[#131](https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/pull/131) found that the tested HNSW layout did not serve tenant reads and had recall and stale-version problems. Adding the same index is not the solution. Evaluate immutable indexed generations plus recent changes for large tenants, but require evidence that the index is used and that filtered recall holds before making that layout part of the serving path. [ClickHouse documents](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/annindexes) both filter trade-offs and index-building cost during inserts and merges.

Version the complete retrieval contract: embedding input and dimensions, lexical tokenization and ranking, filters, fusion, candidate budgets, reranking and temporal rules. Evaluate exact identifiers and phrases, semantic paraphrases, multilingual queries, negation, conflicting revisions, expiry and sparse tenants. Model size or exact vector-neighbor recall alone is not evidence of better final relevance or agent outcomes. Compare candidate generators, embedding and reranking choices on the same evaluation set; the existing path is a control, not a quality ceiling. Choose the strongest measured end-to-end quality that meets the declared capacity and latency requirements, then optimize p99 without lowering the quality gates. Keep citations tied to the validated source revision and test abstention when evidence is insufficient.

Build model and index changes as separate ClickHouse serving generations. Backfill, replay intervening changes and erasures, compare quality against the baseline, prove reader visibility, then atomically switch the Postgres serving manifest. A request pins one compatible model and generation until completion or timeout; retire a generation only after its readers drain. Never compare vectors from incompatible models. Retain a verified generation for rollback only within erasure and retention rules. Measure concurrent rebuild load and bound the recent-change set so it cannot become an unbounded exact scan.

Use [`pg_clickhouse`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/pg_clickhouse/blob/main/doc/pg_clickhouse.md) for unified SQL and analytical queries where the installed version pushes the work down. Keep native ClickHouse queries for the initial serving path. Check `EXPLAIN` before routing a query through Postgres: unsupported filters can prevent limit pushdown, and SQL compatibility alone says nothing about the cost.

#### Tenant placement and database branching

Tenant placement belongs to this architecture; [#157](https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/issues/157) consumes its routing and isolation contract. A tenant is the customer organization represented by `org`. A contract requiring a separately isolated workspace can register its owned namespace set as an explicit placement unit. Neither a user nor an agent/session automatically creates a new database.

| Boundary | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Tenant or registered workspace placement | Region, capacity, authority epoch, and shared or dedicated Postgres service |
| Namespace and collection | Project/content scope and sharing within the tenant |
| User and agent | Grants, private content and permitted actions within those scopes |

Use shared Postgres shards for ordinary tenants and a dedicated always-on service when measured load, residency or the isolation contract requires it. Dedicated placement means an independently sized service with the required HA configuration, not merely `CREATE DATABASE` inside the same resource pool. Personal accounts may have one user and one tenant; that does not make database-per-user the organization model. Keep users who collaborate on documents and memory within the same transactional placement unless an explicit isolation contract requires otherwise.

Route ordinary tenant transactions to one Postgres shard and colocate their transactional dependencies. Promote large tenants to dedicated services when measured load requires it. Managed Postgres offers vertical scaling and read replicas; horizontal write sharding remains a Loom placement decision ([scaling](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres/scaling)). Keep APIs, authoritative transactions, retrieval and validation in the tenant's home region to avoid inter-region round trips in ordinary requests.

Tenant placement includes a durable authority epoch. A move or shard split copies a consistent state, catches up required deliveries, fences and drains the old writers, verifies the destination and switches the route under a bounded write pause. Stale routers and workers cannot write through the old epoch. Split a large tenant only along independent transaction and admission scopes; cross-scope invariants do not become safe merely because the rows moved to separate shards.

Dedicated Postgres does not replace application isolation. Continue to bind every query and job to the identity tuple, current grants and placement epoch. ClickHouse, object storage and caches keep their own scoped access and placement contracts; a Postgres endpoint does not automatically isolate the rest of the product.

Evaluate Xata for dedicated-service provisioning, migration/CI environments and tenant sandboxes. Xata describes copy-on-write branches with independent compute ([branching](https://xata.io/postgres-branching)). That is a candidate capability, not a decision to replace ClickHouse Managed Postgres or a reason to create an instance for every tenant. Keep the first implementation path above until a provider comparison establishes the required guarantees.

Production services with interactive latency SLOs stay warm. Permit hibernation only for profiles whose declared SLO includes wake-up and cache warming; test reconnection storms and whether replication/background connections prevent idling ([scale-to-zero lifecycle](https://xata.io/scale-to-zero)). Copy-on-write reduces the cost of cloned unchanged blocks, not the compute and distinct data of thousands of independently active tenants.

Create new tenants from a clean schema/template. Never clone a shared multi-tenant production database into a new customer's security boundary. Data-bearing test branches stay within their tenant's authorized boundary, with anonymization or synthetic fixtures where required.

A Postgres branch is not a complete Loom fork. Register an environment/branch identity and pin a consistent baseline of database revisions, ClickHouse serving generations and artifact manifests. Use separate writable projection destinations, job claims and external-effect destinations. Cloned outbox rows, credentials or erasure jobs must not execute against production. An older copy of grants cannot restore revoked production access. Branch promotion uses the same fenced, reconciled cutover as any other authority change; do not assume automatic merging of business-state mutations.

Manage the fleet with bounded active-tenant connection pools, migration orchestration, credential rotation, per-source CDC progress, backups, failover and retirement. Budget source/replication connections, compute including HA, storage divergence and catch-up capacity at the expected number of concurrently active tenants. Database-per-tenant improves isolation and placement options; it does not remove a hot namespace's semantic coordination limit or establish better retrieval relevance.

Before changing the provider or placement default, qualify durability and failure-domain behavior, primary failover/fencing, PITR, regional availability, fleet limits, and the selected CDC path. A PostgreSQL-compatible endpoint does not prove access to the physical WAL and recovery state WalShadow requires. Report warm and wake-up latency, sustained mixed load, noisy-neighbor effects and full operating cost against the shared-shard baseline. Track all retained branches in erasure and backup recovery inventories.

#### Batching, capacity and retention

Use a bounded number of enrichment writers per ClickHouse destination shard and table, shared across API replicas. Batch by rows, bytes and a bounded deadline. Avoid stacking a long application timer on top of a long ClickHouse async-insert timer. Prioritize work that a caller is waiting to search.

Validate vector dimensions and partition counts before sending a block. Isolate bad rows, retry ambiguous inserts with stable identities, and apply backpressure when queues or merges fall behind. Leased job claims carry fencing generations so overlapping workers cannot advance progress for a newer claim. Use stable revision, chunk, model and destination identities for logical deduplication: ClickHouse insert-deduplication windows are finite and are not a permanent exactly-once guarantee. Verify retry behavior after the window, across rebatching and with dependent materialized views ([insert retry limits](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/operations/insert/deduplicating-inserts-on-retries)).

Use separate concurrency limits, connection pools and scheduling shares for interactive admissions, searches, archival delivery, imports and rebuilds. Enforce per-tenant and global bounds on outstanding work and provider calls; reserve capacity for interactive work without starving repair and erasure. Count overload rejections and timeouts in service-level results. Bulk work must not exhaust interactive capacity, and overload must not silently select a weaker model or skip a quality check.

Separate ClickHouse retrieval compute from analytics and heavy index construction. Avoid one partition per namespace in shared tables. Keep historical revisions out of ordinary live retrieval. High-volume best-effort telemetry can be buffered directly into ClickHouse; it should not require a Postgres transaction for each metric.

The revision journal has bounded retention after required delivery, not a time-based permission to drop undelivered data. Confirm archive completeness and payload hashes before removing source payloads. Reconciliation detects missing revisions, not just duplicate rows. Retain enough delivery state to rebuild serving data from the journal or confirmed archive. If archival delivery stalls, apply backpressure before storage or WAL retention is exhausted rather than discard history.

The archive consumes immutable revision events with a key that includes source identity and revision; a current-row mirror cannot preserve every revision. Routine source cleanup is not erasure. Configure and test archival handling of source `DELETE`, partition retirement, `TRUNCATE` and `DROP`: WalShadow tees also receive destructive DDL, so mirroring a journal and truncating it can remove the archive. Keep archive lifetime independent of source cleanup, with explicit erasure through Loom's erasure workflow ([destination behavior](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/544c340d17039d2b24068897c6f616b9e67e1ac6/docs/destination-tables.md)). Durable memory and retained history expire only under writer-authorized deletion or retention policy.

Size journal, WAL/archive retention, vector writes and ClickHouse merges from sustained rates, payload bytes, chunk fan-out, content-changing fraction, model rebuilds and outage recovery time. Include per-shard validation lookups, all retrieval legs, generation retries and reranker concurrency. Report normal and catch-up capacity with headroom; peak API throughput alone does not establish sustained capacity.

#### Failure, erasure and rollout

- With ClickHouse unavailable, point reads and operations independent of semantic retrieval continue. Semantic admissions and strict search fail explicitly.
- With Postgres unavailable, authoritative mutations and access decisions fail closed. Do not serve a stale ClickHouse copy as current content.
- Worker restarts replay versioned jobs. Late enrichment cannot overwrite a newer revision. Readiness and job completion survive lost acknowledgements and overlapping claims.
- Deletes and access changes take effect through Postgres authority. Erasure first fences the affected generation, then drains all in-flight publishers or rejects their writes at the destination before cleanup and the final residue check. Expiring a worker lease alone does not establish that quiescence. A check immediately before an unfenced insert cannot prevent a worker from writing after erasure completes. Apply the fence to imports, index builds, CDC recovery and restore as well as enrichment.
- The erasure inventory includes Postgres content, revisions, jobs, idempotency payloads, ClickHouse vectors, graph and text projections, archives, replication recovery state and caches. Preserve deletion evidence across the backup recovery window. Restore in quarantine and apply erasures before serving or replaying jobs. State backup expiry or cryptographic-erasure rules and distinguish live-data completion from backup retention obligations.
- Use synchronous Postgres HA across failure domains for acknowledged-write durability. For Managed Postgres, select two HA standbys; its documented one-standby configuration is asynchronous. Verify the actual commit and promotion policy, including fencing the old primary and choosing a standby that preserves acknowledged commits ([HA options](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres/high-availability)). Replica count alone is not a durability proof.
- Test automatic source failover with the selected WalShadow build. Its planned switchover procedure does not cover abrupt primary loss. Define a bounded recovery or rebootstrap procedure for replication, while retaining all source revisions not confirmed in the archive; a fresh snapshot of current content cannot reconstruct revisions already removed from the source journal. Quarantine or remove abandoned-timeline output before trusting the recovered archive; a larger replication cursor is not proof of valid history. Production acceptance requires that procedure to meet the history durability and recovery objectives.
- Restore both stores with compatible authority epochs and serving manifests. Reconcile source revisions, erasure state and delivery gaps before advertising readiness. Define separate recovery-point and recovery-time objectives for primary/AZ failure and regional disaster; do not present a regional backup policy as zero-loss synchronous HA.

Moving write authority breaks the existing rolling-upgrade assumption that all shared state is in ClickHouse. Seed Postgres from a consistent snapshot, reconcile changes, verify identities and versions, then switch authority under a controlled write pause. Shadow comparisons must not repeat external side effects. Any duplicate inference needs an explicit benchmark budget. Old and new authorities must not accept writes for the same scope. Deploy and verify fencing-capable APIs and workers before cutover while the old authority is still active. Drain or deny storage writes from any older binary that cannot enforce the fence; a new configuration row cannot stop a binary that never reads it. Enforce the authority epoch at admission and commit on every remaining writer. Once the new authority accepts writes, rollback requires a fenced, reconciled reverse cutover; changing a configuration flag is not a rollback. Update the architecture and rolling-upgrade rules with the implementation.

#### Implementation and acceptance

Split the work into:

1. Postgres current-content storage, provenance, atomic audit, admission generations and revision/job/idempotency contracts.
2. Direct search projection, bounded batching, idempotent recovery, reader-visible barriers and explicit API outcomes.
3. WalShadow qualification, retained history, reconciliation, erasure and failover/restore procedures.
4. Search quality validation, model-generation rollout, SDK behavior and fenced authority cutover.
5. Tenant placement, fair scheduling, capacity qualification and any large-tenant index changes justified by measurements.

These are implementation workstreams, not permission to cut over before history, erasure and recovery pass. Keep the existing serving path until the required gates pass for the intended deployment profile.

Define a deployment profile and numeric acceptance thresholds before capacity qualification: tenant and eligible-set distributions, content sizes, write mix, chunk counts, model versions, candidate limits, concurrency, freshness contract, failure domain, hardware and replicas. Keep the existing operation budgets, including the 200 ms p99 target for `memory.set`, as targets to test; they are not results of this proposal. Establish separate end-to-end SLOs for current point reads, semantic admission, strict search, deferred visibility, failover and archival recovery. Report provider-inclusive latency and service-only time separately without excluding queueing, visibility waits, retries or errors from the relevant SLO.

Release gates:

| Gate | Required evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Isolation and correctness | No observed cross-tenant or unauthorized disclosure, lost acknowledged mutation, mismatched revision score, skipped protection, duplicate logical side effect or erased-content resurrection in the correctness and fault suites. Any occurrence blocks release. |
| Retrieval and answer quality | Paired evaluation against the existing retrieval path and exact eligible-set vector results, plus labeled relevance, citation accuracy, abstention and downstream agent outcomes. Set minimum filtered recall and non-inferiority margins per required query and tenant slice before testing; aggregate averages cannot hide a failing slice. |
| Semantic admission | Concurrent same-key and cross-key writes, new peers, pin/blacklist changes, intra-batch conflicts and model failures produce the promised inline verdicts; record false accepts, false refusals and retry rates. |
| Sustained capacity and latency | Mixed traffic at each advertised rate, including admission retrievals, all query legs, validation and model calls. p95/p99 and error rates meet the declared SLOs while queues, journal/WAL storage, dead tuples and parts remain bounded. Include hot scopes, large tenants and small tenants sharing capacity. |
| Degraded operation | Imports, model/index rebuilds, provider throttling, lost replicas, source failover and archive outages preserve correctness and tenant scheduling. Report degraded capacity, recovery backlog and catch-up time. |
| History and recovery | Every required revision and audit event is reconciled across initial load, cleanup, duplicate delivery, restart, source promotion and restore. Validate payload hashes, source epochs and deletion evidence before readiness. |
| Placement and branches | Shared and dedicated profiles pass the same isolation, durability and semantic tests. Tenant moves, stale routes, forked jobs, branch erasure and provider failover cannot cross tenant/environment boundaries. Qualify fleet-scale provisioning, migration, warm latency and any advertised wake-up profile before changing defaults. |

Run at a fixed offered load long enough to exercise checkpoints, autovacuum, merges, journal cleanup and archival delivery, then inject failures and measure catch-up. Report achieved throughput, rejection/timeout counts, CPU, memory, I/O, lock waits, generation retries, queue age, projection lag and parts/merge load. Use representative content and tenant filters as well as synthetic stress data; record queries, seeds, configuration and execution plans so comparisons can be repeated.

Test delivery on replicated ClickHouse tables and every supported serving engine. Cover ambiguous commit and insert responses, out-of-order completion, gaps in readiness, retry after deduplication expiry, replica rerouting, poison rows, expired leases, interrupted tenant moves, planned and abrupt source promotion, erasure racing a publisher, model-generation cutover and recovery from backup. No enterprise capacity, latency or durability claim is accepted from an untested configuration.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- **Postgres heads with content in ClickHouse.** This keeps ClickHouse insertion on the write path and adds a second database lookup to each point read. Storing current content in Postgres removes both dependencies for point operations.
- **Waiting for CDC before enrichment starts.** This adds replication lag before embedding and search publication. Enrichment can read the committed revision directly.
- **A custom general replication pipeline.** WalShadow supplies the native replication path. Loom needs domain-specific enrichment and readiness, not another WAL transport.
- **ClickPipes.** Reconsider it if a documented or reproduced WalShadow limitation blocks a required guarantee. Qualify WalShadow first and do not build both replication paths in parallel.
- **Vectors in Postgres or another search database.** Out of scope. Vector storage and execution remain in ClickHouse.
- **One owner API replica per namespace.** This ties availability to process placement. API replicas remain interchangeable; durable coordination belongs in Postgres.

### Where the need comes from

The need is mine, an AI tool helped shape the proposal

### Additional context

This is an architecture proposal. The review checks the contracts against the linked replication, HA and retrieval evidence; it does not establish measured capacity or production readiness. No new load or recall measurements were run for this revision. The sizing inputs remain assumptions. Implementation and release require the quality, isolation, durability, latency, capacity and recovery gates above.

items.title: Client read architecture: normalized object pool + partial-bootstrap load strategies (Linear-style)
items.body:
## Context

Tracking two pieces of Linear's sync-engine **client architecture** that Lunora intentionally does *not* mirror (noted while reaching feature parity on optimistic rebasing in PR #72). Neither is a gap in correctness — they're different architectural choices, captured here as possible future directions.

### 1. Normalized client object pool

**Linear:** a single normalized in-memory object pool (MobX observables) — every model instance is stored once and referenced everywhere, so a delta updates one object and all views re-render.

**Lunora:** per-subscription query *results* (each `useQuery` holds its own value) plus a durable read cache, reconciled via CDC deltas/snapshots. Simpler, no normalization layer; the cost is that the same entity appearing in N queries is materialized N times.

### 2. Partial bootstrap with per-model load strategies

**Linear:** `/sync/bootstrap?type=full|partial` with per-model load strategies (`instant` / `lazy` / `partial`) and sync groups — only the models a view needs are loaded.

**Lunora:** per-subscription snapshot + cursor/epoch resume; the read cache hydrates last-seen data on boot. No model-level `instant`/`lazy`/`partial` granularity.

## Why out of scope

Both are large architectural investments that pay off mainly at very large client datasets. Lunora's per-subscription model is sufficient (and simpler) for the target workloads today.

## What to revisit (if ever)

If apps hit memory pressure or slow cold-bootstrap from large datasets, a normalized store and/or partial bootstrap become worth evaluating.

items.title: Add "Architecture" section under Guides & References / Backend Development: monolith vs. microservices (benefits, drawbacks, when to use each), backend/frontend layering with API gateway and BFF, migration paths (legacy stack → modern, monolith → modular monolith → microservices, single-tenant → SaaS), a "starting a new project" technology guide, and a cheat sheet PDF
items.body:
## Summary

Add a new **Architecture** documentation section at **Guides & References / Backend Development**, as a sibling
of the existing Hibernate, SpringBoot, GraphQL, Spring Batch, OAuth, Quarkus, Messaging and Architectural
Patterns references (`modules/ROOT/pages/backend/architecture/`), following the exact structure/conventions of
those sections: a landing page with a **Bibliography** section, **one page per concept** explored in the two
requester-provided books (each with the disclaimer partial, a `== References` section linking the online
documentation the concept derives from, and Mermaid/SVG figures), and a one-page, printable, downloadable
**Architecture cheat sheet PDF** styled like the existing `architectural-patterns-cheat-sheet.pdf` /
`messaging-cheat-sheet.pdf`.

The section answers four questions the site does not answer today:

1. **Monolith or microservices?** — what each architectural style actually is, the **benefits** of microservices
   (independent teams and services; small, fast-to-evolve, independently deployable and scalable services;
   fault isolation; freedom to adopt new technology) and their **inconveniences** (loss of ACID transactionality
   and of globally consistent queries, distributed-system and operational complexity, far more code and
   infrastructure to maintain, cross-service feature coordination, the difficulty of finding the right service
   boundaries), and **when each one is the better choice** — monoliths for small projects, small teams, one-shot
   deliveries and applications that will not need to evolve much; microservices for large, complex, long-lived
   systems that must scale, be developed by several autonomous teams, or need per-component scaling for
   performance reasons.
2. **How to layer an architecture** so backend and frontend evolve independently: a REST (or GraphQL/gRPC) API
   behind an **API gateway** / **backends-for-frontends**, completely separate web frontends (React, Angular,
   Vue) that consume that API, and native mobile apps consuming the very same API — versus server-rendered UIs
   and when those still make sense.
3. **Migration paths** — from legacy technology stacks to modern ones, from monoliths to modular monoliths and
   to microservices (the **strangler fig** application, the three refactoring strategies, integration glue and
   anti-corruption layers, splitting the domain model and the database, sequencing extractions so the monolith
   never needs compensating transactions, adapting security), and from single-tenant installed software to
   multi-tenant **SaaS** (silo lift-and-shift, layered migration, service-by-service migration, and the
   silo/pool deployment models).
4. **Which path and which technologies to pick for a brand-new project**, chosen among the technologies already
   documented on this site, based on the expected project profile: large or small, low or high traffic, one-shot
   vs. long-term maintenance and evolution, one team vs. many, need for native apps, need for multi-tenancy.

Pages 3 and 4 (the migration paths and the "new project" guide) must be written in an **easy, simple-to-follow
style, with worked examples, Mermaid diagrams and SVG figures** and with **links to recommended external sites**
as proof of the explained concepts and as a way to obtain further information. For the other pages Mermaid/SVG
figures are not mandatory — add them only where they genuinely help.

* `benefits-and-drawbacks.adoc` — **What microservices give you and what they cost you.** The benefits of the
  monolithic architecture while the application is small (simple to develop, easy radical changes, simple
  testing and deployment, easy X-axis scaling) and the symptoms of **monolithic hell** as it grows (complexity
  intimidates developers, slow edit-build-run-test loop, long commit-to-deploy path with manual testing and
  monthly releases, conflicting resource requirements make scaling hard, no fault isolation, locked into an
  obsolete stack). The **benefits of microservices**, each explained with the Bookshop example: continuous
  delivery/deployment, small easily maintained services, **independent deployability**, **independent
  scalability** (CPU-hungry search vs. memory-hungry catalogue), **autonomous "two-pizza" teams** owning services
  end to end, easy experimentation with and adoption of new technologies, fault isolation. The **inconveniences**:
  finding the right set of services is hard and getting it wrong produces a distributed monolith; distributed
  systems are complex (IPC instead of method calls, partial failure, latency, retries, circuit breakers); **loss
  of ACID transactionality** — sagas, eventual consistency, no cross-service joins (API composition / CQRS) —
  linking to the Architectural Patterns pages for the mechanics; **higher complexity and much more code and
  infrastructure to maintain** (service chassis, observability, service discovery, gateways, per-service
  pipelines, contract tests, security tokens, distributed IDs — each linked to the existing page that documents
  it); features spanning services need coordinated rollouts; higher operational and skills bar; deciding when to
  adopt is itself hard. 📊 side-by-side comparison table; 📊 SVG `architecture-monolithic-hell.svg` (the
  downward spiral: growth → complexity → slower delivery → more pressure).
* `choosing-monolith-or-microservices.adoc` — **When a monolith is the better choice and when microservices
  are.** A plain-language decision guide: a monolith (modular from day one) for small projects, small teams (one
  team that fits around a table), one-shot deliveries and prototypes, applications that will not need to evolve
  much, startups still searching for their business model ("a startup should almost certainly begin with a
  monolithic application" — Richardson; MonolithFirst — Fowler), strict transactional domains, and anywhere the
  operational prerequisites (automated deployment pipeline, monitoring, rapid provisioning — Fowler's
  MicroservicePrerequisites) are missing; microservices for large, complex, long-lived systems developed by
  several autonomous teams, for **performance and scale** reasons when components have very different resource
  and scaling profiles, when fault isolation or independent release cadence is a business requirement, when
  parts of the system need a different technology stack, and for consumer-facing or SaaS products at scale. The
  "is it really the architecture?" check: slow delivery and buggy releases are often a **process** problem
  (manual testing, no CI/CD) — fix that first (Richardson 13.1.1). Signals that it is time to split (the
  monolithic-hell symptoms as a checklist) and signals that it is time to **merge back** (the Prime Video
  monitoring case study: chatty services and per-call infrastructure cost). 📊 Mermaid decision flowchart; 📊
  table "project profile → recommended style" that the new-project guide later expands.

### Layering the architecture

* `layering-backend-and-frontend.adoc` — **Isolating backend and frontend so they evolve independently.**
  From the classic monolith that renders HTML pages to a **backend that exposes only an API** (REST by default;
  GraphQL/gRPC where the existing comparison pages say so) **behind a gateway**, consumed by **completely
  separate web frontends** (React, Angular, Vue — each linked) and by **native mobile apps** (Android/Kotlin,
  iOS/Swift, or cross-platform) that use the very same API; why this lets the frontend team iterate, A/B-test
  and release without touching the backend, lets several UIs share one backend, and opens the door to native
  apps and partner integrations; what it costs (CORS, two deployables, API versioning, contract-first with
  OpenAPI — link to `api-first-rest-and-grpc.adoc` —, SEO/SSR, authentication via the **BFF** — link to the
  OAuth browser-based-apps page); when **server-rendered UIs** (Thymeleaf, Vaadin, Blazor Server, JSF) are still
  the right, simpler choice (internal tools, small teams, content sites, one-shot projects); server-side rendering
  frameworks (Next.js/Nuxt/Angular SSR) as the hybrid; **micro-frontends** named in one paragraph with links, not
  documented. The Bookshop example: one Spring Boot API, one React web app, one Android app. 📊 SVG
  `architecture-layered-target.svg` (browser SPA + native apps → gateway/BFF → API → services/database); 📊
  Mermaid sequence diagram of one "place order" request crossing the layers; 📊 table "UI approach → when to use".
* `api-gateway-and-bff.adoc` — **API gateway and backends for frontends.** Why clients should not call services
  directly (many round-trips, no encapsulation, unsuitable protocols); the API gateway as the single entry point
  — request routing, API composition, edge functions (authentication, rate limiting, TLS, logging), protocol
  translation —, its benefits and drawbacks (one more highly available component, risk of becoming a development
  bottleneck); the **backends-for-frontends** variant (one gateway per client type owned by the client team, the
  Netflix story), and when one gateway is enough; **implementation options** with links: off-the-shelf (AWS API
  Gateway, Kong, Traefik, Envoy / Kubernetes Gateway API, NGINX) vs. building your own (Spring Cloud Gateway,
  YARP), GraphQL as a gateway (link to the GraphQL federation / when-to-use pages); the gateway during a
  migration as the **strangler's routing seam**. 📊 Mermaid figure of gateway vs. BFF topologies; a ~20-line
  Spring Cloud Gateway route example routing `/api/orders/**` to the extracted Order service and everything else
  to the monolith.

### Migration paths

* `migration-overview.adoc` — **How to approach any migration.** The **balancing act** between business
  motivators (competition, operational cost, new markets, customer demand) and technical desires (erase technical
  debt, shiny new stack) — the strategy must be driven by the business (Golding); **timing**: "modernize first"
  vs. "deliver now, modernize incrementally", and why early customer feedback usually wins; the **fish model** of
  costs and revenue during a transformation; **no big bang rewrite** ("the only thing a Big Bang rewrite
  guarantees is a Big Bang"), the **strangler fig** as the universal shape of every path in this section;
  **demonstrate value early and often**; **minimize changes to the legacy system**; **don't build the deployment
  infrastructure up front** — an automated deployment pipeline with automated tests is the only thing you can't
  live without; a **time-boxed target-architecture definition** (a couple of weeks) as the destination; and the
  five **pitfalls** every path warns about (big bang, distributed monolith, shared database, premature
  infrastructure, forgetting the organisation and process side). Ends with a **"where are you? → which page"**
  table that maps the reader's current situation (legacy stack monolith / healthy monolith that has outgrown
  itself / modular monolith / partially extracted / single-tenant installs) to the following four pages. 📊 SVG
  `architecture-strangler-over-time.svg` (the monolith shrinking while the strangler application grows); 📊
  Mermaid figure of the fish model; 📊 Mermaid flowchart "which migration path".
* `migration-path-legacy-to-modern-stack.adoc` — **From a legacy technology stack to a modern one** (without
  necessarily changing the architectural style). Typical starting points and their modern targets, as a table
  with links to the existing references: Java EE / Struts / JSP / Spring 3-4 XML → **Spring Boot** or
  **Quarkus**; .NET Framework Web Forms / MVC 5 → **ASP.NET Core** (link to the existing Web Forms migration
  page); jQuery/server-templated UI → **React / Angular / Vue** SPA or a server-rendered modern framework;
  SOAP/ESB → **REST / gRPC + messaging**; stored-procedure business logic → application-layer domain model;
  legacy ORM/JDBC → **Hibernate / Spring Data**; ad-hoc deployment → containers and a pipeline. The techniques,
  each explained simply with the Bookshop example: the **strangler fig with a reverse proxy / gateway** in front
  of the legacy app (route by path, header, or user cohort; YARP, NGINX, Spring Cloud Gateway), **separate the
  presentation tier from the backend first** (Richardson's second strategy: expose the business logic as an
  API, then rebuild the UI as a SPA against it — the seam every later step reuses), **branch by abstraction**
  and **parallel run** (legacy-displacement patterns), the **anti-corruption layer** between old and new models,
  **data synchronisation** during the overlap (dual writes vs. CDC with Debezium — link), **incremental
  framework upgrades** when the stack is upgradable (Spring's backward compatibility) vs. strangling when it is
  not, feature flags and cohort-based cut-over, and the **exit criteria** for decommissioning the legacy system.
  📊 Mermaid flowchart of the strangler routing (proxy → legacy vs. new); 📊 SVG
  `architecture-presentation-backend-split.svg` (monolith with UI → API backend + SPA); 📊 step-by-step table
  "week 0 → week N" for the Bookshop UI migration.
* `migration-path-monolith-to-modular-monolith.adoc` — **From a big-ball-of-mud monolith to a modular
  monolith** — the safest first step of any microservices migration and, for many teams, the final destination.
  Identify modules by business capability / subdomain (link to Strategic Design), draw the **target module map**,
  enforce boundaries (packages + **Spring Modulith** `@ApplicationModule` and its verification tests; ArchUnit;
  .NET projects), replace cross-module object references and shared tables with **module APIs and in-process
  domain events** (Spring Modulith events — the outbox in a single database), give each module its own schema
  or table prefix so the database can later be split, kill **god classes** by splitting them per module, and
  measure coupling. Why this already buys most of the maintainability benefits at none of the distributed cost,
  and the **signal to go further**: a module needs its own release cadence, scaling profile, team, or stack.
  📊 Mermaid module-dependency graph of the Bookshop before/after; a ~25-line Spring Modulith module + event
  example; 📊 table "monolith → modular monolith → microservices: what you gain at each step".
* `migration-path-monolith-to-microservices.adoc` — **From a (modular) monolith to microservices** — the
  centrepiece of the section, written as a step-by-step guide with the Bookshop example. Richardson's **three
  strategies**: (1) **implement new features as services** ("stop digging" — the Bookshop's new
  recommendations feature is born as a service; when a feature is too small or too coupled to be a service);
  (2) **separate presentation tier and backend** (link back to the legacy page); (3) **extract business
  capabilities into services** — the vertical slice (inbound adapters, domain logic, outbound adapters, schema),
  **splitting the domain model** (object references → ids, extracting `Shipment` out of the `Order` god class),
  **refactoring the database** (split table, move table), **replicating data back to the monolith** to avoid
  widespread changes, and **what to extract first** (rank by: accelerates development, solves a
  performance/scaling/reliability problem, unblocks other extractions; "freeze the monolith and extract on
  demand" vs. the planned backlog). **Designing how the service and the monolith collaborate**: the integration
  glue (repository-style interface for queries, service-style interface for commands), querying the monolith via
  REST vs. keeping a **replica fed by events**, updates via **transactional messaging**, the **anti-corruption
  layer** in both directions, **how the monolith publishes domain events** (inserting publish calls vs.
  transaction-log tailing/CDC when the monolith can't be changed — link to Kafka Connect / outbox) and subscribes
  to them (helper application when it can't). **Data consistency between monolith and service**: why splitting
  an ACID transaction forces a saga, why the monolith is often an unwilling saga participant (compensating
  transactions need semantic-lock states scattered across the monolith), the rule "**keep the monolith's
  transactions pivot or retriable**", and **sequencing the extractions** so the monolith never needs a
  compensating transaction (the Bookshop sequence: Order → Customer → Catalogue/Inventory → Payment, each shown
  as the resulting saga) — linking to the Architectural Patterns saga page for the saga mechanics themselves.
  **Security**: from session cookies to a user-info cookie/token propagated by the gateway (link to OAuth
  pages). **Deployment**: a service at a time, containerised, on whatever the team already runs; Kubernetes only
  when there are enough services to justify it (link). Closing checklist per extracted service. 📊 SVG
  `architecture-extract-service.svg` (vertical slice leaving the monolith, gateway routing, integration glue); 📊
  Mermaid sequence diagrams for the Bookshop "place order" saga before and after extracting Payment (monolith as
  pivot); 📊 Mermaid figure of query-by-API vs. replica-by-events; 📊 table of extraction order with the reason
  for each step.
* `migration-path-to-multi-tenant-saas.adoc` — **From single-tenant installed software to multi-tenant SaaS.**
  Why this is a distinct path (it changes the business, not only the code); the **control plane / application
  plane** split and why the control plane (onboarding, identity, tenant management, metrics, billing, admin) is
  built first — "**build your multi-tenant foundation on day one**"; **tenant context** flowing through every
  request (routing, logging, data access, isolation); the **silo / pool** vocabulary and the deployment models
  (full-stack silo, full-stack pool, hybrid with a premium siloed tier, mixed mode per service, pods); the three
  **migration patterns** with the Bookshop-as-a-SaaS example — **silo lift-and-shift** (fastest, least
  invasive, one version for everyone, automated per-tenant onboarding), **layered migration** (pool the web
  tier, then the application tier), **service-by-service migration** (strangle the application tier into
  pooled multi-tenant microservices, "don't compromise on the new microservices", integrating legacy code with
  the control plane) —, their pros and cons side by side, the **phased approach** that chains them, "**where you
  start matters**" (identity → onboarding → tenant authentication → tenant context in services → tenant-aware
  logs and metrics), and the guiding principles (**avoid the tech-first trap**, no one-size-fits-all, protect
  the multi-tenant principles). Links to the AWS SaaS Lens and the SaaS Architecture Fundamentals whitepaper as
  the primary online sources, and to the Hibernate multitenancy page for the data-partitioning mechanics. 📊 SVG
  `architecture-saas-migration-patterns.svg` (the three patterns side by side over control plane + application
  plane); 📊 Mermaid figure of the phased approach; 📊 table silo vs. pool vs. hybrid vs. mixed vs. pod with
  "when to use".

### Starting from scratch

* `starting-a-new-project.adoc` — **Which path and which technologies to use for a new project**, chosen among
  the technologies documented on this site. First the **profile questions** (expected size and domain
  complexity; expected traffic — low, high, bursty; lifetime — one-shot vs. long-term maintenance and evolution;
  number of teams; need for a public API, native apps, several UIs; need for multi-tenancy; compliance; team
  skills and budget), then the **default path**: start as a **modular monolith with a clean API layer** and a
  separate frontend when there will be more than one client, extract services only when a signal from the
  "choosing" page appears; then **scenario cards**, each with a one-paragraph story, the recommended
  architecture, a recommended stack drawn *only* from documented technologies with links to the existing
  comparison pages, and what to explicitly *not* do: (a) **small one-shot project / internal tool** (a
  monolith, server-rendered UI or a small SPA, one relational database, single JAR/container or PaaS, no
  Kafka, no Kubernetes); (b) **startup MVP that must evolve fast** (modular monolith, REST API + React/Angular/Vue
  from day one so native apps can follow, PostgreSQL, container on a managed platform, feature flags); (c)
  **long-lived line-of-business application for one organisation** (modular monolith with Spring Modulith or
  Quarkus, RabbitMQ for background work, OAuth/OIDC, observability from day one); (d) **high-traffic consumer
  application** (API gateway/BFF, microservices for the hot paths only — search on Elasticsearch/Solr, catalogue
  cache, order/payment sagas —, Kafka, Kubernetes, CQRS read models — links to the Architectural Patterns
  pages); (e) **large multi-team enterprise platform** (microservices by business capability, API-first
  contracts, gateway + BFF per client, event-driven integration, per-service databases, distributed tracing);
  (f) **multi-tenant SaaS product** (control plane first, pooled application plane, tiering; serverless for the
  control plane where traffic is low); (g) **batch / data-processing job** (Spring Batch, no web layer at all —
  link). Cross-cutting recommendation tables with links: backend framework (Spring Boot vs. Quarkus; Java vs.
  Kotlin; Python/FastAPI where the GraphQL section already documents it), API style (REST vs. GraphQL vs. gRPC),
  messaging (Kafka vs. RabbitMQ — or none), database (link to Choosing the Right Database), frontend
  (React/Angular/Vue vs. Vaadin/Blazor/Thymeleaf; Bootstrap vs. Tailwind), mobile (Kotlin/Android, Swift/iOS,
  cross-platform in one line), authentication (OAuth/OIDC, BFF for SPAs), deployment (single process → container
  → managed container platform → Kubernetes → serverless: what each is good for, with the serverless long-tail
  latency caveat for JVM services and Quarkus native as the mitigation). 📊 Mermaid decision flowchart
  (profile → style → deployment); 📊 SVG `architecture-project-profile-matrix.svg` (the scenario × concern matrix
  in one picture); 📊 one small Mermaid topology figure per scenario card.

### Reference

* `cheat-sheet.adoc` — describes the sheet and links every section page, plus
  `xref:attachment$architecture-cheat-sheet.pdf[Download the Architecture Cheat Sheet (PDF)]`.

## Cheat sheet (`modules/ROOT/attachments/architecture-cheat-sheet.pdf`)

Exactly **one A4 page**, landscape or portrait like the existing sheets, produced with the established
mechanism (hand-built HTML/CSS → headless Chromium → PDF, HTML not checked in), visually consistent with
`architectural-patterns-cheat-sheet.pdf` / `messaging-cheat-sheet.pdf` (same colour-coded boxes, fonts and
footer). Content, **built around "where are you now? → what to do"**:

* **Migration paths by current architecture** — one row per starting point: *legacy-stack monolith* (proxy +
  strangler; split presentation from backend first; ACL; CDC for data overlap), *healthy monolith that outgrew
  itself* (modularise first: modules by capability, Spring Modulith, in-process events, per-module schema),
  *modular monolith with a hot spot* (extract that capability: new features as services first; vertical slice;
  ids not references; replicate data back; gateway routes; keep the monolith pivot/retriable; extraction order),
  *partially extracted system* (sagas/outbox/CQRS per Architectural Patterns; consolidate the gateway/BFF; retire
  the monolith or keep it as one more service), *single-tenant installs* (control plane first → silo
  lift-and-shift → layered → service-by-service; silo/pool per service).
* **Monolith vs. microservices** signal box — choose a monolith when…, choose microservices when…, "is it really
  the architecture?" check, signals to split, signals to merge back.
* **Benefits / inconveniences** two-column box (microservices).
* **Layering** box — SPA + native apps → gateway/BFF → API → services; when server-rendered UI is fine.
* **New project → recommended stack** matrix — the seven scenario cards of `starting-a-new-project.adoc` in one
  compact table (architecture, backend, API, messaging, database, frontend, mobile, deployment), each cell
  naming documented technologies only.
* **Pitfalls** strip — big bang, distributed monolith, shared database, premature Kubernetes, tech-first SaaS.
* **Pointers** — the microservices.io, martinfowler.com, Azure/AWS/GCP guidance URLs, and the two books.

## Cross-links to add in existing pages

* `backend/index.adoc` — new "Architecture" bullet in `== Sections`; description/keywords updated.
* `backend/architectural-patterns/index.adoc` — one sentence in the intro pointing to
  `xref:backend/architecture/index.adoc` for the monolith-vs-microservices decision and the migration paths
  (that section explicitly declared "strangler migration" out of scope; this is where it now lives).
* `backend/springboot/architectural-patterns.adoc` — its *Where this section stops* paragraph gains a pointer to
  the new section for migration and layering.
* `web/aspnet/web-forms/migrating-to-modern-aspnet.adoc` — one sentence pointing to
  `xref:backend/architecture/migration-path-legacy-to-modern-stack.adoc` for the technology-neutral strangler
  strategy.
* `web/aspnet/core/architecture-and-patterns.adoc` — its modular-monolith bullet links to
  `xref:backend/architecture/migration-path-monolith-to-modular-monolith.adoc`.
* `backend/oauth/browser-based-apps.adoc` — one sentence pointing to `api-gateway-and-bff.adoc` for the BFF as an
  architectural (not only security) pattern.
* `database/choosing-the-right-database.adoc` and `backend/graphql/when-to-use-graphql-or-rest.adoc` — a
  "see also" line pointing to `starting-a-new-project.adoc`, which composes them.
* `modules/ROOT/pages/index.adoc` — keywords only.

## Bibliography additions

* The new `backend/architecture/index.adoc` gets its own `== Bibliography` following the Architectural
  Patterns format (*Pattern catalogues and canonical articles*, *Cloud-provider architecture guidance*,
  *Technology documentation*, *Consulted reference books*) listing **every** link in the "Online sources"
  section above plus the two books (Richardson — Manning page; Golding — O'Reilly page with the Amazon fallback
  and the free AWS whitepaper) and the further-reading titles (Newman; Ford et al.; Richards & Ford; Ambler &
  Sadalage), each with the note on how it was used, and the closing sentence that the books are consulted
  references only and the online catalogues are authoritative on any discrepancy.
* `backend/architectural-patterns/index.adoc#_bibliography` — under *Consulted reference books*, extend the
  Richardson entry's note to say that chapters 1, 2, 8, 12 and 13 are the narrative source for the sibling
  Architecture section, and add Golding's book with the same links as above (it is the source of the
  multi-tenancy angle that the Hibernate multitenancy page and the new SaaS page share). No other existing
  bibliography needs changes.

## Out of scope

* Re-documenting anything in the table above (DDD tactical patterns, sagas/outbox/CQRS mechanics, REST vs.
  GraphQL vs. gRPC, Kafka vs. RabbitMQ, database selection, OAuth flows, Kubernetes/serverless mechanics,
  Spring Boot vs. Quarkus) — all linked.
* Service discovery, circuit breakers, service mesh, distributed tracing, contract testing, the microservice
  chassis — named in one sentence with a link where a page touches them (the "what it costs you" page and the
  new-project deployment table), not documented.
* AWS-specific mechanics from Golding's chapters 4–12 and 14–16 (Cognito, EKS/Lambda implementations, tiering,
  SaaS Anywhere, GenAI) — only the deployment models, migration patterns and guiding principles are used.
* Micro-frontends beyond one paragraph with links; a full tutorial for any gateway product, Spring Modulith or
  YARP (each is shown in one short snippet at most and linked).
* Organisational/process transformation (team topologies, DevOps adoption) beyond the sentences the migration
  overview needs to say "this is not only a technology change".
* Cost modelling and cloud pricing.

## Task details

* **Importance**: important.
* **Estimated difficulty**: hard — 13 concept pages plus a landing page and a one-page PDF, of which the five
  migration/decision pages carry a hard "simple to understand, with worked examples, Mermaid and SVG figures"
  requirement and must stay mutually consistent on one running example; the material itself is stable and
  well-sourced, the cross-linking surface is large (nine existing sections are linked), and every recommended
  technology must be one this site already documents. No new tooling is needed; the Architectural Patterns and
  Messaging sections provide a complete precedent for structure, disclaimer, figures and the PDF pipeline.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `modules/ROOT/partials/architecture-disclaimer.adoc` exists, contains **only** the AI-assistance
      disclosure and the bibliography pointer, and no other admonition block
      (`NOTE`/`TIP`/`WARNING`/`CAUTION`/`IMPORTANT`) appears anywhere under `modules/ROOT/pages/backend/architecture/`
      other than that include.
- [ ] `modules/ROOT/nav.adoc` has the Architecture block under *Guides & References → Backend Development*,
      after the Architectural Patterns block; `backend/index.adoc` lists "Architecture" as a new bullet with
      updated `:description:`/`:keywords:`; the root `pages/index.adoc` keywords mention monolith, modular
      monolith, microservices, strangler fig, migration, API gateway, BFF and SaaS.
- [ ] All 13 concept pages + `index.adoc` + `cheat-sheet.adoc` exist under
      `modules/ROOT/pages/backend/architecture/`, each with `:description:`, `:keywords:`, the disclaimer include
      and a `== References` section linking only online documentation; every technology a page recommends is one
      already documented on this site and is linked to its existing reference page.
- [ ] The pages answer explicitly, with the arguments from the books and the linked online sources: **what**
      microservices give you (independent teams and services, small and fast-to-evolve independently deployable
      units, independent scaling, fault isolation, technology freedom), **what** they cost (loss of ACID
      transactionality and consistent queries, distributed-system complexity, more code and infrastructure to
      maintain, coordinated cross-service rollouts), **when** a monolith is better (small projects, small teams,
      one-shot, no need to evolve, missing prerequisites) and **when** microservices are (large, complex,
      multi-team, long-lived systems; performance/scaling of large systems), and **how** to layer backend and
      frontend so they evolve independently and native apps can share the API.
- [ ] The five migration/decision pages (`migration-overview.adoc`, the four `migration-path-*.adoc` pages) and
      `starting-a-new-project.adoc` are written in plain, step-by-step language, share the Bookshop running
      example, each contain at least the 📊 figures listed (Mermaid and SVG under
      `modules/ROOT/images/architecture-*.svg`), and each provide links to recommended external sites as proof
      and further reading for every migration technique and every technology recommendation.
- [ ] `starting-a-new-project.adoc` covers at least the seven scenario cards (small one-shot / startup MVP /
      long-lived line-of-business / high-traffic consumer / large multi-team platform / multi-tenant SaaS /
      batch job) and the cross-cutting recommendation tables, with every recommendation linked to the existing
      comparison page it derives from.
- [ ] `npm run validate:mermaid` passes for every Mermaid block in the section.
- [ ] `index.adoc` has a `== Bibliography` section listing and linking every source in the groups above,
      including both books with their publisher pages and the note on how they were used, and the Architectural
      Patterns bibliography is extended as described.
- [ ] `modules/ROOT/attachments/architecture-cheat-sheet.pdf` exists, is exactly one A4 page, covers every box
      listed under "Cheat sheet" — in particular the "migration path by current architecture" rows and the
      "new project → recommended stack" matrix —, is visually consistent with the existing cheat sheets, and is
      linked from `cheat-sheet.adoc` via `xref:attachment$…`.
- [ ] The cross-links listed under "Cross-links to add in existing pages" are in place.
- [ ] `npx antora antora-playbook.yml` builds with no `xref` or AsciiDoc errors and
      `build/site/backend/architecture/` renders every page, every SVG and the PDF download.

items.body:
Part of epic #172.

## Task

Build the reusable production test harness that wires:
- **Real containers**: Postgres, DuckDB, MinIO/S3 via testcontainers
- **Real CDC flusher**: `internal/cdc` package, not harness-simulated export
- **Real federated engine**: `internal/federated` package, not custom SQL
- **Real schema metadata**: load from schema JSON, register in schema registry
- **Real manifest store**: S3-backed manifest, not in-memory

## Diagnostic output

Every test failure must produce a run-specific artifact directory with:
- Fixed random seed + run ID
- Test fixture / event log
- `change_log` snapshot
- S3 object listing
- Manifest raw JSON
- Parquet schema + sampled rows
- Generated production SQL, parameters, and execution plan
- Expected vs actual diff
- `KEEP_E2E_ENV=1` keeps containers alive for manual inspection

## Oracle model

Build an **independent expected-state model**:
1. Collect events by `row_id`
2. Pick latest version
3. Apply deletions
4. Apply filters
5. Sort
6. Paginate

Do NOT reuse the federated engine to compute expected results.

## Constraints

- Each test owns isolated schema ID, tenant, bucket prefix

items.title: Epic: Stateful inference migrations — verified embedding generation changes, cutover, rollback, and release evidence
Decision: where cloud state lives — Cloudflare only (A) or Convex for catalog/app state (B); Convex-for-everything ruled out

labels.name: decision
labels.description: A choice the founders need to make

items.body:
## Question
Where does each part of Signalbox's cloud state live, and on which platform? Per #840, every part sits behind a module interface, so this is a choice of adapter, not a rewrite. T3 Code's thread model stays as it is.

## Options
- **A. Cloudflare only.** Thread DOs (items plus live stream), a catalog in D1 or Postgres with our own sync for the sidebar, R2, and an external search engine.
- **B. Convex for catalog and app state** (folders, roles, thread list and status, presence, notifications, usage ledger, automation records), **plus Cloudflare for thread items and the live stream**, R2 and external search.
- **C. Convex for everything**, including thread items and live deltas. Cloudflare only for runners, ModelGateway, Dynamic Workflows and R2.

In every option, runners, ModelGateway with the CLIProxyAPI pools, Dynamic Workflows (sandboxed user automation code) and R2 or S3 stay on Cloudflare. Convex's AI Gateway can't front CLIProxyAPI, and its VM components (including Boat's) can't replace MachineBackend.

## Cost premium over A ($/user/month, month 12, measured usage)
"Heavy" is one real dogfood user's measured T3 Code and Codex history. "Typical" is 1/5 of that. Every formula and price is in the design notes (cost-premium.md).

| | Heavy, 100 users | Heavy, 5,000 users | Typical, 100 | Typical, 5,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **B over A** | +$0.78 | +$0.64 | +$0.40 | +$0.27 |
| **C over A** | +$12.87 (Pro) | +$4.80 (Business, dedicated) | +$3.76 | +$1.75 |
| C with Convex's built-in search | +$36 | about +$1,100 | +$46 | about +$5 |

- C's premium is mostly live streaming. One-second updates are billed as Convex calls for every watching device; on DOs the same traffic costs about $0.01. Keeping the stream on a DO cuts C to about +$2.50–3.10.
- Convex's built-in search bills every query for the whole shared index, so it's ruled out as the history index.
- Most uncertain inputs: the live delta rate, how many devices watch a stream, whether DOs really sleep between messages, and Convex's billing for built-in indexes.

## Other findings that shape this
- Per-thread DOs aren't the flaw; using them as the only database is. Every actor-per-entity system pairs its actors with a central index (Temporal, Restate, Rivet, tldraw, Cloudflare's Agents SDK). Missing today: a catalog, a search index fed from threads, a thread-to-thread inbox (Warp's protocol shape), and a fix for the resume bug behind "Syncing messages…" (#779).
- Convex-style layers on Cloudflare: Lunora is closest to the right design (per-DO writer, index-range invalidation, per-tenant sharding), but it's one maintainer, about 509k lines, not Effect. Concave speaks Convex's protocol on DOs but is unmaintained compiled code with a single writer. Concile isn't really Convex-compatible. Building our own is estimated at 10–15k lines and 3–6 months to production.
- Lock-in exits: self-hosted Convex (Postgres) for B and C; celld (Apache-2.0) runs Workers and DOs on our own machines for A and B.
- Search, in every option: one logical index partitioned by content home and assembled per query from the searcher's current access. It covers excerpts, not full tool output, keyword first. The engine is turbopuffer or our own SQLite FTS, pending a spike.

## Recommendation
**C is out**: +$5–13 per heavy user, which is significant by Yannic's yardstick. **A vs B is the real choice**: B costs about $0.30–0.80/user more and buys Convex's DX and live sync for the catalog and app layer, which is where cross-thread features live. A is cheapest and has no second vendor, but we build catalog sync ourselves (Lunora-style).

Lean: **B**, behind the #840 catalog module interface, so it can later move to self-hosted Convex or our own DO layer without touching features. Thread items and the stream stay in DOs. Fix the resume protocol (#779) and add the thread inbox and search index now, since those are needed in A or B.

## Decision needed (Yannic)
- [ ] A or B?
- [ ] Thread search before this lands: a throwaway on today's stack now, or wait?

## Sources
The research records on this issue, on #847 (Convex on Cloudflare), on #791 (one index) and on #788 (history measurement).
